items.content:
@TimDarcet @gabriberton The P in JEPA stands for predictive.
The main distinction is not between JEA and JEPA, but between Joint Embedding (predictive or not) and generative architectures.
Whether a predictor is necessary depends on the task.

Given observations x and y (y being available only during training), a generative architectures predicts y from x. The loss is the divergence between y and its prediction:
  L = divergence(y, pred(enc(x)) )

A JEA encodes y as well and minimizes the divergence between the representations of x and y, while preventing collapse:
  L = divergence( enc(y), enc(x) ) + R( enc(y), enc(x) )
Where R is the anti-collapse regularizer, which may be computed over a batch of samples.
JEA are used when the prediction has no particular direction, i.e. when x and y are different views of the same scene. The idea for JEA is very old. Becker and Hinton proposed a simple model in 1989 where the anticollapse was based on information maximization. Schmidhuber had a version in 1992 based on redundancy minimization. At NIPS 1993, I proposed Siamese nets, which was a contrastive method to train JEA. Such contrastive methods gained popu.arity after Google's SimCLR paper in 2020. In 2021, Stéphane Deny in my group proposed the Barlow Twins redundancy reduction regularizer, which seemed to work at scale. This was shortly followed by VICReg by Adrien Bardes, Jean Ponce, and me, and last year by SIGReg by Randall Balestriero and me. 
DINO is a JEA method that comes from a long string of papers from Piotr Bojanowski's group at FAIR-Paris, starting with Noise as Targets (2017), Deep Clustering (2018-2020), and DINO v1-v3 which are contrastive between clusters, not samples.

JEPA adds a predictor, which is useful when the prediction is non-symetric. For example, when x is a degraded/corrupted version of y, or when x is a present observation and y a future observation (temporal prediction). The loss is:
  L = divergence( enc(y), pred(enc(x)) ) + R( enc(y), enc(x) )

All of these models can be augmented by an action variable a, fed to the predictor, encoding an action, intervention, or transformation to produce y from x.
This turns the system into a "world model". In a JEPA, the loss becomes
  L = divergence( enc(y), pred(enc(x), a) ) + R( enc(y), enc(x) )

items.content:
🪦 RIP 

🫟 Infinite Slop TV

August 2026 - October 2026

It let anybody on the internet write into a chat that fed into a perpetual stream of live generated AI video (aka slop)

It wasn't possible before that because there weren't AI video models yet that generated faster than they could be played, but then @fal hacked @MiniMax_AI's H3 to be so fast that it finally could! FAL also sponsored me to do this project because otherwise it would have costed me $200,000/mo in GPU cost, at least!

Here's some stats:

📈 17,800,000 clip views
💬 287,555 chat messages
❤️ 287,000 likes on clips
📺 210,196 AI clips aired
🛡 125,808 messages blocked by moderation 💀 (so about 44% was blocked!)
👀 185,000 visitors
💬 47,000 people made videos
⏱ 860 hours of never-repeating video
💰 3 sponsors: @sideshiftai + @creem_io + @chatbase

Paid out 3 prizes: 
🏆 $5000 to "67" (wanted to stay anon)
🪙 $2500 to @ssthormess (aka "SS" on the site)
🥉 $1000 to @tatusea_ ("tatusea" on the site)

In the end it didn't manage to keep catching attention though but it was a great little fun internet experiment

Lots of funny weird things happened, because each video generated would take cues from the previous (the AI would try keep some type of cohesion), you'd get these kind of trends keep going through videos. For awhile every video had goth girls, then slime girls, then pickles, then it'd turn into pixel art, and then people would spam it back to goth girls

There is something here though, but I'm not sure what it is, or how to make it work in the future. Slop is of course slop, and it is addictive but after awhile it also gets boring because it's still too basic. I can see that there will be interactive and personalized content in the future that's live generated and will work but we're not there yetttt

It's also a bit dystopian but utopian in other ways: live generated teachers explaining stuff to kids is awesome for example and I think I saw Minimax H3 Max used for that too

Anyway, everyone thanks for watching and creating! 🙏😊

Introducing the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2: a new proprietary evaluation, updated benchmarks, and a headline metric that rewards model calibration

We’ve released the second version of the Artificial Analysis Decision Index to better reflect real-world utility and guard against benchmark gaming. 45% of the Index is now built on private datasets, up from 25% in v1. Drex Max v1.1 from @NaceAI narrowly leads among decision models at 73, within 1 point of GLiDE v1.2 (@fastinoAI) and Mammoth 27B (@baselabs)

Updates in Decision Index v2:

➤ Decision Score: We adopt a new headline metric that rewards a model for both correctness and calibrated confidence. Each question scores from 0 to 100: right answers score above 50, wrong answers below 50, and confidence in its top answer moves the score within each half

➤ AA-Paperclip (30%): We added a new private benchmark of 1,500 documents including resumes, receipts, invoices, and AI and machine learning research papers. Models make decisions and extract facts from each document and are scored jointly as a single decision, correct only if all 15 answers are right

➤ AA-Symmetry (15%): This evaluates whether models change their answers for equivalent questions worded differently. We test 120 questions with variations such as reordered options, swapped labels, and negated yes/no questions, then measure how consistent the model’s probabilities are across those variations

➤ AA-Omniscience-Decision v1.1 and HLE-MultiChoice v1.1 (15% each, down from 25%): AA-Omniscience-Decision now varies the wording of its “I don’t know” option across ten alternatives. HLE-MultiChoice adds an option to decline using the same ten phrasings

We’ve also added EvalSafe-ONET-AA (15%), our implementation of @typesafeai’s ONET benchmark. We have retained When2Call from @NVIDIAAI in the Index at a decreased weighting of 10% (down from 25%), and removed WildGuardTest given its high saturation

Key results:

➤ Three decision models sit within 1 point at the top of the Index: Drex Max v1.1 from Nace AI and GLiDE v1.2 from Fastino Labs both score 73, with Mammoth 27B from Base Labs scoring 72

➤ Cost per 1M Tasks varies by more than 60x across decision models: Celeris-1.1 Decision ($14), Decider v1.2 ($68) and Drex Max v1.1 ($102) sit on the Decision Index vs. Cost Pareto frontier, while Clef costs $859. Token price is not the only cost driver: most decision models, including Drex Max v1.1 and Decider v1.2, bill a document’s input once for all its questions, while GLiDE v1.2 and Decider Flash v1.2 bill it for every question. This means GLiDE v1.2 costs $780, nearly 8x higher than Drex Max v1.1 despite only 33% higher list prices

➤ Language models can score higher, alongside higher Cost and Time per Task: Claude Haiku 5.5 (Max) scores 77 and GPT-6 Luna (Max) scores 76 on Decision Index v2, putting them ~3 points ahead of Drex Max v1.1. GPT-6 Luna (Max) costs $1,530 per 1M Tasks vs. $102 for Drex Max v1.1 (15x the cost) and takes 11.34 seconds per task vs. 275 milliseconds (~40x slower)

items.title: AA-Paperclip tests models on extracting facts and making decisions about real-world documents. Each ...
items.content:
AA-Paperclip tests models on extracting facts and making decisions about real-world documents. Each of its 1,500 private documents has five decisions and ten facts to extract. The key metric measures the share of documents where a model answers all 15 questions correctly. For the Decision Score, the model’s confidence in a document is the product of its 15 answer probabilities.

Claude Haiku 5.5 (Max) passes 92% of documents and GPT-6 Luna (Max) passes 86%. Drex Max v1.1 (63%) and GLiDE v1.2 (62%) lead the decision models, followed by Decider v1.2 (55%). The all-pass requirement separates models that look close on individual answers. Drex Max v1.1 gets 97% of answers right, close to Claude Haiku 5.5 (Max) at 99%, but passes 63% of documents against Haiku's 92%. Decision models lose most documents on the decisions rather than extraction, with Drex Max v1.1 correctly making all five decisions on 71% of documents and all ten extractions on 88%.

items.title: The Decision Score rewards models for both correct answers and well-calibrated confidence. A decisio...
items.content:
The Decision Score rewards models for both correct answers and well-calibrated confidence. A decision model’s answer is typically acted on when its confidence clears a threshold; otherwise, it is passed to a person or a more capable model. The Decision Score measures the average payoff across all thresholds, so it does not depend on choosing a single cutoff.

For each question, the score is 50 × (1 + c − (p − c)²), where p is the probability the model assigns to its chosen answer and c is a flag for whether the answer was correct (c = 1 if correct, c = 0 if incorrect). Across an evaluation, this is equal to 50 × (1 + Accuracy − Brier score).

Including confidence impacts overall leaderboard rankings. On AA-Paperclip, for raw accuracy Clef passes 36% of documents and Celeris-1.1 Decision passes 24%, but Celeris-1.1 Decision matches it on the Decision Score due to better calibration (Brier score of 0.15 vs. 0.27 for Clef). Across the Index, GLiDE v1.2 leads Drex Max v1.1 on accuracy metrics (60 vs. 58), while Drex Max v1.1 edges ahead on the Decision Index.

items.title: Generating images sequentially from left to right—known as autoregressive next-token generation—mirr...
items.content:
Generating images sequentially from left to right—known as autoregressive next-token generation—mirrors how LLMs generate text, making it highly attractive for building unified AI systems across text, speech, and vision. However, when applied to images using continuous numerical representations (latents) produced by standard image autoencoders, autoregressive models have consistently lagged behind diffusion models and bidirectional masked generators. The fundamental cause is that standard continuous latents vary widely in scale across dimensions and tokens. During sequential generation, these scale discrepancies amplify step by step, an effect severely exacerbated by steering methods like classifier-free guidance, ultimately causing generative failure and degraded image quality.

The article demonstrates that this instability can be resolved by enforcing scale invariance across all autoregressive steps. To achieve this, the authors introduce SphereAR, a framework that constrains all latent tokens—both inputs fed into the model and generated outputs—to lie on a fixed-radius hypersphere, thereby eliminating scale degrees of freedom and stabilizing the sequential generation process.

items.title: AA-Symmetry measures how consistent models are when asked equivalent questions. We take a fixed task...
items.content:
AA-Symmetry measures how consistent models are when asked equivalent questions. We take a fixed task set and make changes like reordering options, swapping labels, or negating yes/no questions. AA-Symmetry includes 120 base questions and total 440 variations, testing consistency in both the chosen answer and its probability.

Models from @baselabs lead on AA-Symmetry, driven by a high abstention rate. They consistently admit they do not know an answer with high confidence across question variations, earning high consistency scores. Mammoth 27B scores 96 and Elephant 9B scores 93 on AA-Symmetry. Mammoth 27B selects the same answer across variations on 99% of questions, compared with 91% for Drex Max v1.1, 88% for GLiDE v1.2 and 67% for Clef.

items.content:
Decision model costs ranged from $14 per 1M Tasks for Celeris-1.1 Decision to $859 for Clef. Celeris-1.1 Decision, Decider v1.2 and Drex Max v1.1 sit on the Decision Index vs. Cost Pareto frontier, with GPT-6 Luna (Max) ($1,530) and Claude Haiku 5.5 (Max) ($6,240) extending it at higher scores.

Token price isn’t the only factor in decision model cost. GLiDE v1.2 and Decider Flash v1.2 evaluate each question in a separate pass and bill the input each time, so an AA-Paperclip task uses about 63k input tokens, against about 9k for Drex Max v1.1. As a result GLiDE v1.2 costs $780 per 1M Tasks at $0.04 per 1M input tokens, and Decider Flash v1.2 costs $196, nearly 3x Decider v1.2, at half its token price.

items.title: Modern reasoning-oriented AI models achieve high performance by generating extensive intermediate ch...
items.content:
Modern reasoning-oriented AI models achieve high performance by generating extensive intermediate chains of thought, but this process demands substantial computational resources and frequently leads models into unproductive, overthinking paths. Standard approaches to ensure answer reliability typically involve generating multiple outputs and aggregating them via majority voting or querying separate verifier models. However, these techniques scale computing costs linearly or worse, while simple heuristics like output confidence or response length fail to reliably distinguish successful reasoning from erroneous wandering.

The article demonstrates that tracking the internal representational movement of a model—termed Latent-Trajectory signals—provides an accurate, training-free method to predict solution correctness and streamline inference. The overarching objective is to evaluate whether measuring how a model's hidden states evolve across tokens can reliably forecast answer accuracy and cut inference compute without degrading performance.
